subtype: Approach: making questions and answering from memory [Thinking]
passage: Note from the Class 6 tutor, Thursday evening. Sahil sat with his science book and a pencil. Sahil made a question out of every heading. The one on seasons became, "Why is winter colder than summer?" Then he closed the book and answered aloud. "Because the earth is far from the sun?" He stopped, frowned and opened the book. "No. The tilt changes how the light falls." He ticked the right ones and put a cross by the wrong ones. Then he went back to read only the crossed topics. I did not tell him the answers. I only asked what he would study again. Himani, tutor

qa.q: What question did Sahil make from a heading?
qa.a: He asked, "Why is winter colder than summer?"

qa.q: What did Sahil feel when he stopped, frowned and checked the book after his first answer?
qa.a: He felt unsure and a bit puzzled, since he suspected his answer was wrong. Checking gave him the right idea.

qa.q: What alternative approach could Sahil use to check his answers, and why?
qa.a: He could ask a friend to ask the questions from the book. Hearing someone else's questions covers parts he may not think to ask.

qa.q: How does the tutor Himani see Sahil's method?
qa.a: Himani sees a boy who finds his own gaps and works on them, which is why Himani only asked what he would study again.

grounding: A boy turns each heading into a question and answers aloud with the book closed, and checking wrong answers tells him exactly what to study again.

subtype: Approach: making questions and answering from memory [Thinking]
passage:
Thursday, 9 pm
Geography test tomorrow. Today I tried something new. I turned every heading into a question and wrote them on a page. 'What causes the seasons?' 'What makes day and night?' 'Why is it hot near the equator?' Then I shut the book and answered each one out loud to the wall. Hansa didi laughed from the doorway. 'Nitin bhai, are you teaching the wall?' Seasons: I said it was because the Earth goes nearer the sun in summer. I checked. Wrong! It's the tilt. So I read that part again, twice, and answered again. Now I know exactly which bit I didn't get.

qa.q: What did Nitin first say causes the seasons?
qa.a: Nitin said it was because the Earth goes nearer the sun in summer.

qa.q: How did Nitin feel when the check showed the answer was wrong?
qa.a: Nitin seemed surprised but pleased, since the wrong answer showed exactly which part to study again.

qa.q: What could Nitin do with the questions tomorrow morning?
qa.a: Answer them all once more from memory before school, and re-read only the ones he gets wrong.

qa.q: How does Hansa see Nitin's method?
qa.a: Hansa finds it funny and teases Nitin about teaching the wall, without knowing how useful it is.

grounding: Shows a child turning headings into questions, answering aloud with the book closed, and using a wrong answer to see what to study again.

subtype: Approach: making questions and answering from memory [Thinking]
passage: The electricity had gone in the village again, so Omkar sat on the stone step of the temple with his science book and a hurricane lamp. Hemant, his little brother, sat beside him. 'Hold the book, and don't let me see it,' Omkar said. He had written the headings as questions in his small notebook. 'What do roots do? Why do leaves turn to the sun? How does water climb up a plant?' He answered each one out loud. Hemant followed along in the book. 'Wrong on the last one,' Hemant said. Omkar nodded slowly. 'So that's the one I read again tonight. The others I know.'

qa.q: Where did Omkar sit to study?
qa.a: On the stone step of the temple, with a hurricane lamp.

qa.q: Why did Omkar nod slowly when Hemant said he was wrong?
qa.a: He seemed calm and satisfied rather than upset, because the mistake told him exactly what to read again.

qa.q: What could Omkar do if Hemant isn't around to hold the book?
qa.a: Write the answers on the back of each question and check them himself after answering from memory.

qa.q: What is the study session like for Hemant?
qa.a: Hemant gets an important job, checking the answers in the book, so he's part of the work and may feel proud to help.

grounding: Illustrates a child turning headings into questions, answering aloud without the book, and checking wrong answers to know what to reread.
